# Part plan

- Kettle: rounded tapered ivory vessel with a narrow cylindrical neck, a bent open light-wood handle, and an ivory hollow gooseneck spout. These components form one rigid body.
- Base: a low ivory control plinth with a round heating/docking surface, a dark circular display, a brass-coloured control knob, and subtle grey control symbols. One separate rigid body.
- Lid: inset ivory disk with a short wide knob, independently modelled and initially seated.

Use photo contours to refine body proportions and supplied calibrated cameras for offline image comparisons. The first nominal rest image shows the vessel held above the base; its supplied static transform does not describe that displaced state. Several segmentation masks exclude visible accessories. Evaluate the main body on views 1–4 and document full-mask scores separately.

# Completed asset

`model.blend` contains three named visual rigid bodies, with eight hidden compound collision children. `model.glb` contains only the three visual bodies and embedded maple texture. OBJ parts and collision meshes use metres and +Z up in the same shared frame. The canonical origin is the horizontal centre of the complete asset bounds at its lowest point. Blender body pivots use estimated centres of mass. The glTF exporter converts to +Y up.

The total asset envelope is approximately **0.210 × 0.277 × 0.207 m**. The main vessel diameter is **0.158 m**, vessel height **0.178 m**, and top rim is **0.192 m** above the support plane. The supplied 0.16 × 0.16 × 0.187 m reconstruction box agrees approximately with the vessel itself, but does not include the full photographed handle, spout and control plinth. These were reconstructed from their relative photo proportions, so the complete asset deliberately exceeds the measured box. Depth and accessory dimensions remain assumptions.

The visible base consists of a rectangular control plinth and a round docking/heating plate, represented as one rigid body. The kettle can lift, translate and rotate freely; `joints` is empty because a prismatic joint would incorrectly constrain the demonstrated motion. The separate lid is seated but detachable. No cable is included because the visible background cables cannot be assigned confidently to this object.

# Registration and review

The five calibrated cameras use their supplied intrinsics and OpenCV transforms, converted to Blender convention. A single translation, recorded in `model.json` as `asset_to_capture_translation_m`, maps the normalized asset frame to the supplied reconstruction frame. No per-view camera corrections are applied. This translation is necessary because the fitted resting object lies below and behind the nominal measured-box origin. Canonical exports do not bake in this translation.

`review.jpg` shows all five source/render pairs and the in-hand reference with an explicit unknown-camera note. Transparent renders are composited over grey. `renders/beauty.png` is an additional inspection view. View 0 depicts the person holding the kettle above the base; its static supplied object pose does not explain this displacement, so it is retained in the review but excluded from the fit statistic. The in-hand image has no pose and cannot provide a calibrated silhouette comparison.

The final mean vessel-only silhouette IoU is about **0.918** on views 1–4 (roughly 0.956, 0.915, 0.899, 0.901). These compare the actual rendered vessel mesh with accessory-excluding targets at one-third resolution. View 1 and 2 targets remove the handle from the supplied masks; view 3 uses a manually traced vessel contour to exclude base/spout clutter; view 4 uses the supplied mask. The saved targets and exact method are in `evaluation/` and `evaluation.json`. This is a fitting diagnostic on the same views used to build the model, not an independent reconstruction accuracy measurement.

Unmodified whole-mask IoUs are approximately 0.50, 0.67, 0.74, 0.72, 0.74. They do **not** reach 0.85: several input masks omit accessories and the entire base while the complete render includes them. The displaced view 0 is another source of mismatch. The body threshold should not be interpreted as whole-object silhouette success.

# Materials and contact assumptions

- Vessel: warm ivory coated metal, moderately rough finish. Hollow-looking top and spout outlet are visual approximations; the vessel interior is closed below the lid. The main vessel collision is a filled convex hull, shortened below the lid seat to avoid penetration. It cannot simulate water, internal tools, or a hand entering the vessel.
- Handle: light maple appearance, recreated longitudinal grain in `textures/maple_basecolor.png`, attached rigidly to the kettle. Two solid convex pieces preserve the handle opening. Grain is procedural, not recovered wood grain. Hidden attachment hardware is omitted.
- Spout: curved ivory tube with a recessed visible outlet. Three convex solid pieces approximate the arc. Collision thickness is about 9 mm; no thin shell collision is used. The lumen is visual only and pouring is not simulated.
- Lid: separate disk and short knob, one filled convex collider with approximately 19 mm total thickness. No inferred latch or hinge is added. The rim does not constrain sideways lid motion in the simplified physics.
- Base: ivory plinth, round docking disk, dark unlit circular display, brass-coloured dial and faint geometric controls. The single 11 mm thick convex base collider gives a stable support slab; small raised controls and feet do not receive individual collision shapes. Illegible branding and text were not invented.
- Dry mass guesses: kettle 0.75 kg, lid 0.07 kg, base 0.35 kg. Effective assembly density guess: 350 kg/m³; this is an envelope density, not steel density. Friction 0.55, collision margin 0.5 mm on child hulls, estimated body centres of mass. The base is passive/anchored in Blender, and the kettle and lid are active. Change the base to active if independent base motion is required.

All **8/8** collision meshes are convex, watertight and have positive volume, checked with trimesh. The visual asset has **18,456 triangles**, below the requested 60k limit. A 120-frame settling test at 24 fps, 10 substeps and 30 solver iterations left the kettle and lid seated, with about 1 mm and 2 mm vertical settling respectively. This checks basic assembly stability only, not material calibration or task success. Results are saved in `evaluation/collision_checks.json` and `evaluation/physics_settle.json`.

# Remaining mismatches and reproducibility

The spout azimuth, base depth, handle cross section and obscured bottom are estimated from limited views. The model cannot match moving view 0 with the same rigid pose as the resting views. Lighting in the source is warm and spatially uneven; studio render colours therefore differ, especially on the upper shoulder. Fine writing and exact control icons remain unresolved. The smooth parametric taper is an approximation of the photographed body.

Run `~/blender/blender -b -P build.py` to regenerate all geometry, texture, Blender/GLB/OBJ files and camera renders. The fitted parameters are embedded in the standalone build script; `fit.json` and `fit_body.py` retain the fitting provenance. Run `review.py` in a Python environment with Pillow, NumPy, SciPy and OpenCV to regenerate the comparison sheet and image metrics. Rendering/build timing is recorded in `model.json` (about six seconds for this local headless run, excluding modelling and fitting). All evaluation is **offline**. No online estimation speed, reconstruction video, camera trajectory, or temporal reconstruction has been measured: the provided inputs are static crops and camera poses, not a synchronized capture sequence.
